facts.summary: Non-exempt employees must be paid time-and-a-half for hours over 40 in a workweek. Federal law has no daily overtime.
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division

facts.summary: The executive/administrative/professional (EAP) exemption requires a salary of at least $684/week ($35,568/year), plus the salary-basis and duties tests.
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division
facts.notes: The 2024 final rule (raising to $844 then $1,128/wk) was vacated 2024-11-15 (E.D. Tex.). A technical amendment restored the 2019 $684 text, effective 2026-05-15. Confirm figure annually.

facts.summary: Highly compensated employees ($107,432/year+) are exempt under a relaxed duties test.
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division

facts.summary: Computer employees are exempt if paid at least $27.63/hour (or the salary level) and perform qualifying duties.
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division

facts.summary: Federal minimum wage is $7.25/hour. State or local minimums that are higher apply instead.
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division

value: sex (incl. pregnancy, sexual orientation, gender identity)
facts.summary: Federal law prohibits employment discrimination based on these protected characteristics.
facts.citation: 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2 (Title VII); 29 U.S.C. § 623 (ADEA); 42 U.S.C. § 12112 (ADA); Bostock v. Clayton County (2020)
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission

facts.summary: Title VII and the ADA cover employers with 15 or more employees; the ADEA covers employers with 20 or more.
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission

facts.summary: Employers (15+) must provide reasonable accommodation for a known disability unless it causes undue hardship, and must engage in an interactive process. Medical info must be kept confidential.
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission

facts.summary: It is illegal to retaliate against someone for reporting discrimination/harassment or otherwise engaging in protected activity, even if the underlying claim is not proven, if made in good faith.
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission

facts.summary: Employees have the right to discuss wages and working conditions with coworkers; policies forbidding it are generally unenforceable.
facts.sourceAgency: National Labor Relations Board

facts.summary: A discrimination charge must be filed with the EEOC within 180 days, extended to 300 days where a state/local agency enforces a parallel law. Federal employees must contact an EEO Counselor within 45 days.
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission

facts.summary: FLSA wage claims must generally be brought within 2 years, or 3 years for a willful violation. The clock runs from each unpaid payday and keeps running -- it does not pause while a Wage and Hour Division complaint is investigated. Because each paycheck is treated as a separate violation, waiting on an investigation (or on a demand-letter/negotiation process) before deciding whether to sue can let the oldest unpaid weeks fall outside the window and become unrecoverable in a private lawsuit. Workers considering a private FLSA suit should act well before the deadline rather than assuming a pending WHD complaint protects their right to sue.
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division
facts.notes: Summary extended 2026-08-24 (docs/flsa-process-gap.md G1) to cover continuous-accrual timing and the non-tolling effect of a WHD complaint; value unchanged. See also enforcement.paths.

facts.value: Equal to back wages (effectively doubles recovery)
facts.summary: In a private FLSA lawsuit for unpaid minimum wage or overtime, a worker who prevails can recover the unpaid wages PLUS an equal additional amount as liquidated damages -- effectively doubling the wage recovery -- unless the employer proves to the court's satisfaction that it acted in good faith and had reasonable grounds to believe its pay practice complied with the law. This is separate from, and in addition to, the underlying back wages.
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division
facts.notes: Added per docs/flsa-process-gap.md (G2). As of June 27, 2025 (WHD Field Assistance Bulletin 2025-3), WHD no longer seeks liquidated damages in administrative/investigation-stage back-wage settlements -- this liquidated-damages remedy is available through a private §216(b) lawsuit (or a court judgment in a Secretary of Labor suit), not through the administrative complaint process alone. See enforcement.paths.

facts.value: Reasonable attorney's fees + costs awarded to a prevailing plaintiff
facts.summary: A worker who wins an FLSA lawsuit for unpaid wages is entitled to have the court award reasonable attorney's fees and costs on top of the wages and liquidated damages recovered. This fee-shifting rule is why many wage-and-hour lawyers take these cases on a contingency basis (no upfront cost to the worker) -- their fee is intended to be paid by the losing employer, not out of the worker's recovery.
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division

facts.summary: It is illegal for an employer to fire, demote, cut hours, or otherwise punish a worker for asking about, complaining about (even informally or only verbally), or filing a wage/overtime claim under the FLSA -- whether the complaint goes to the employer internally, to the Wage and Hour Division, or to a court. The U.S. Supreme Court held in Kasten v. Saint-Gobain Performance Plastics Corp. (2011) that this protection covers a clear oral complaint, not only a written one. A worker retaliated against may file a WHD retaliation complaint or bring a private suit for relief including reinstatement and lost wages, separate from the underlying wage claim.
facts.citation: 29 U.S.C. § 215(a)(3); Kasten v. Saint-Gobain Performance Plastics Corp., 563 U.S. 1 (2011)
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division

facts.value: WHD complaint (free, back wages only) or private lawsuit (back wages + liquidated damages + attorney's fees)
facts.summary: A worker generally has two ways to pursue unpaid FLSA wages, and choosing one can affect the other. (1) File a free, confidential complaint with the Wage and Hour Division (WHD); WHD can investigate and supervise payment of back wages, but as of June 27, 2025 (FAB 2025-3) WHD no longer seeks liquidated damages in administrative/investigation-stage matters -- the administrative route recovers back wages only. (2) File a private lawsuit under §216(b), which can recover back wages PLUS liquidated damages PLUS attorney's fees and costs, and can proceed as a collective action with coworkers. The two paths interact: a worker who accepts back wages paid under WHD supervision, or whose case the Secretary of Labor has already sued over, may NOT also bring a private lawsuit for those same wages. Because the statute of limitations keeps running during a WHD investigation (see deadlines.flsaWageClaim), waiting on the administrative process before deciding whether to sue carries real timing risk.
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division
facts.notes: Added per docs/flsa-process-gap.md (G3). Administrative liquidated-damages practice change per WHD Field Assistance Bulletin 2025-3 (June 27, 2025), see https://www.dol.gov/newsroom/releases/whd/whd20250627. Private-suit bar upon accepting WHD-supervised payment or a Secretary's suit is 29 U.S.C. § 216(b).

facts.summary: Equal Pay Act claims may be filed within 2 years (3 for willful) and do not require an EEOC charge first.
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission

facts.summary: Eligible employees at employers with 50+ employees (within 75 miles) may take up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for qualifying family/medical reasons.
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Department of Labor, Wage and Hour Division

facts.summary: A worker retaliated against (fired, demoted, etc.) for reporting a workplace safety or health hazard, or for otherwise exercising OSHA rights, must file a Section 11(c) whistleblower complaint with OSHA within 30 days of the adverse action -- much shorter than the EEOC's 180/300-day discrimination-charge window. The complaint can be filed by phone, in writing, or online; no lawsuit or lawyer is required to file it.
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Department of Labor, Occupational Safety and Health Administration
facts.notes: Confirmed 2026-08-08 directly against whistleblowers.gov (statute text: 'within thirty days after such violation occurs, file a complaint with the Secretary') and osha.gov guidance. This is a much shorter, easy-to-miss deadline distinct from the EEOC discrimination-charge deadline (deadlines.eeocCharge, above); route safety-retaliation fact patterns here, not to the EEOC deadline. Some other federal whistleblower statutes OSHA also administers (e.g. certain environmental, trucking, and financial-reform laws) have longer deadlines (90-180 days) -- this 30-day figure is specific to OSH Act Section 11(c) safety retaliation.

facts.summary: For a valid waiver of age claims in severance, workers 40+ get at least 21 days to consider (45 in a group layoff) and 7 days to revoke after signing.
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission

facts.value: no federal rule in effect; governed by state law
facts.summary: The FTC's 2024 rule that would have banned most post-employment non-compete agreements nationwide is not in effect. A federal district court vacated the rule, and on September 5, 2025 the FTC voted 3-1 to dismiss its appeals (Ryan LLC v. FTC, 5th Cir.; Properties of the Villages v. FTC, 11th Cir.) and accede to that vacatur; the rule was removed from the Code of Federal Regulations effective February 12, 2026. Non-compete enforceability is therefore governed entirely by state law (see each state's nonCompete.enforceability fact), though the FTC has said it will continue to evaluate individual non-competes case-by-case under its general unfair-methods-of-competition authority.
facts.citation: 89 Fed. Reg. 38342 (May 7, 2024) (vacated); FTC dismissal of appeals, Sept. 5, 2025
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Federal Trade Commission
facts.notes: This is a status note about the ABSENCE of federal preemption, not a substantive federal non-compete rule -- workers and employers should look to their state's non-compete law (see state files) for the applicable enforceability standard.
